questions.question: How do you declare a variable with a specific type in TypeScript?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use a type annotation after the variable name, such as writing the type after a colon.

questions.question: What is an interface in TypeScript and how do you use it to type an object?
questions.goldenAnswer: An interface defines the shape of an object; you declare it with property names and types, then annotate an object variable with that interface.

questions.question: How can you make a function generic in TypeScript?
questions.goldenAnswer: Declare a type parameter with angle brackets after the function name and use that parameter as the type of the argument and return value.

questions.question: What does the 'readonly' keyword do in a TypeScript interface?
questions.goldenAnswer: It marks a property as immutable after initialization, preventing reassignment.

questions.question: How does TypeScript enforce type safety when assigning a value to a variable?
questions.goldenAnswer: It checks that the value's type matches the declared type and reports an error if they do not match.

questions.question: How can you write a generic function that returns the same type as its argument without using any type assertions?
questions.goldenAnswer: Define a generic type parameter T for the function and use T as the return type, so the compiler infers the argument type and enforces the same type for the return value.

questions.question: What is the difference between an interface and a type alias when defining object shapes, and when would you choose one over the other?
questions.goldenAnswer: Interfaces can be extended and merged across declarations, while type aliases cannot; use an interface when you need declaration merging or to extend existing interfaces, otherwise a type alias is sufficient.

questions.question: How can you allow an object to have a known set of properties but also accept arbitrary additional properties?
questions.goldenAnswer: Add an index signature like [key:string]:unknown to the interface or type, which permits any extra string keys while keeping the known properties typed.

questions.question: What is a type guard and how can you implement one for a custom type?
questions.goldenAnswer: A type guard is a function that returns a boolean and narrows the type in its true branch; implement it by checking a discriminant property and returning a type predicate such as value is MyType.

questions.question: How can you write a function that accepts either a string or an array of strings and internally normalizes the input to an array?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use a union type for the parameter and inside the function check if the argument is a string; if so, wrap it in an array, otherwise use it directly.

questions.question: What TypeScript utility type would you use to make all properties of an interface read-only, and why would you use it?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the Readonly<T> utility type to prevent accidental mutation of objects, which is useful for immutable state or configuration objects.

questions.question: How can you create a type that represents all the keys of an interface that are optional?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use Partial<T> to make every property optional, then extract keys with keyof if needed.

questions.question: How can you extract the type of the value returned by a function type using built-in utilities?
questions.goldenAnswer: Apply the ReturnType<T> utility to the function type, which yields the type of its return value.

questions.question: In TypeScript, how can you enforce that an object passed to a function contains at least one of a predefined set of optional properties, but not necessarily all of them?
questions.goldenAnswer: Define a union of interfaces, each requiring one of the optional properties, and let the function accept that union; this guarantees at least one property is present while keeping the rest optional.

questions.question: How can you create a type-safe wrapper around a Redux action creator that automatically infers the action type and payload type from the original function?
questions.goldenAnswer: Wrap the action creator with a generic that captures its return type using ReturnType and then extract the type and payload fields with conditional types, ensuring the wrapper’s signature matches the original.

questions.question: When rendering a component based on a string key, how can you use TypeScript to map each key to its specific prop type and enforce that the props passed match the key?
questions.goldenAnswer: Define a discriminated union of component prop interfaces keyed by a literal type, then use a generic render function that accepts the key and infers the corresponding props via conditional type mapping.

questions.question: How can intersection types be used to merge two component prop interfaces while detecting incompatible overlapping properties at compile time?
questions.goldenAnswer: Intersect the interfaces and add a constraint that overlapping keys must be assignable to each other; if they are not, TypeScript will emit an error, preventing accidental prop clashes.

questions.question: How do you select an element with the id "header" using vanilla JavaScript?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use document.getElementById('header') to retrieve the element.

questions.question: How can you change the text content of an element that has the class "title"?
questions.goldenAnswer: Select the element with document.querySelector('.title') and set its textContent property.

questions.question: How do you add a new paragraph as a child of a div with the id "content"?
questions.goldenAnswer: Create a paragraph element, set its textContent, and append it to the div using appendChild.

questions.question: How can you remove the last child element of a list with the id "items"?
questions.goldenAnswer: Get the list with document.getElementById('items'), access its lastElementChild, and call remove() on that child.

questions.question: How do you traverse from a button element to its containing form element?
questions.goldenAnswer: Starting from the button, repeatedly use parentElement until you reach an element whose tagName is 'FORM'.

questions.question: How can you efficiently find all elements with a specific data attribute and toggle a class on them without iterating over the entire DOM?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use querySelectorAll to select only the elements with that data attribute, then loop through the resulting NodeList and toggle the class on each element using classList.toggle.

questions.question: Explain a method to remove a node from the DOM that minimizes reflow and repaint costs.
questions.goldenAnswer: Detach the node by calling parentNode.removeChild or element.remove, which removes the node without affecting unrelated parts of the tree, thereby reducing reflow.

questions.question: Describe how to update the text content of a deeply nested element without re-rendering its entire subtree.
questions.goldenAnswer: Select the target element directly, then set its textContent property. This updates only that node and its text, avoiding any reflow of sibling nodes.

questions.question: What is the most straightforward way to find the closest ancestor of an element that matches a given selector?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the Element.closest method, passing the selector string; it returns the nearest ancestor that matches or null if none is found.

questions.question: What are the key differences between innerHTML and textContent when modifying the DOM?
questions.goldenAnswer: innerHTML parses the string as HTML and can inject markup, while textContent sets raw text and is faster and safer because it does not parse HTML.

questions.question: How would you implement event delegation for a list of items that are added dynamically after page load?
questions.goldenAnswer: Attach a single event listener to a static parent element, then in the handler check event.target against a selector to determine if the click originated from a list item.

questions.question: Explain how to replace a node with another node while preserving any event listeners attached to the original node.
questions.goldenAnswer: Clone the original node with cloneNode(true) to copy its listeners, then use replaceChild or replaceWith to swap the old node for the clone, keeping listeners intact.

questions.question: Describe a technique to detect when a specific element enters the viewport and then load its content lazily.
questions.goldenAnswer: Create an IntersectionObserver that watches the element; when the observer reports it is intersecting, trigger the lazy load logic and then unobserve the element.

questions.question: What strategy would you use to remove a large subtree from the DOM while preventing layout thrashing, and why is it effective?
questions.goldenAnswer: Detach the subtree into a DocumentFragment, perform all removals, then replace the fragment with null; this keeps the subtree out of the live DOM so no reflow occurs for each removal.

questions.question: How can you implement a custom diffing algorithm for a virtual DOM that ensures minimal updates to the real DOM, especially when dealing with lists of items that can reorder?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use stable keys to identify items, compare previous and next lists, and only update nodes whose key changed; this prevents unnecessary node creation and preserves component state.

questions.question: Explain how to set up event delegation for a component that dynamically creates and destroys many child elements, ensuring that event listeners do not accumulate and cause memory leaks.
questions.goldenAnswer: Attach a single listener to a stable ancestor, use event.target matching to identify the intended child, and remove the ancestor listener when the component is destroyed; this keeps listener count constant and avoids closures holding onto removed nodes.

questions.question: What approach would you take to traverse a deeply nested DOM to find all elements that match a complex selector while minimizing layout thrashing, and why is this approach preferable?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use querySelectorAll once to get all matches, then process the NodeList in memory; this avoids repeated layout queries and ensures a single reflow for the selector engine.

questions.question: How do you create a promise that resolves after 2 seconds?
questions.goldenAnswer: You can create a new Promise and use setTimeout to call resolve after 2000 milliseconds.

questions.question: What is the difference between using .then() on a promise and using async/await?
questions.goldenAnswer: Both are ways to handle asynchronous results, but .then() registers callbacks while async/await allows you to write asynchronous code that looks synchronous.

questions.question: How does the event loop prioritize microtasks over macrotasks?
questions.goldenAnswer: After a task finishes, the event loop runs all queued microtasks before moving on to the next macrotask, ensuring microtasks execute first.

questions.question: What happens if you throw an error inside an async function?
questions.goldenAnswer: The async function returns a rejected promise with that error, which can be caught with try/catch or .catch().

questions.question: How can you run multiple promises in parallel and wait for all to finish?
questions.goldenAnswer: You can use Promise.all with an array of promises; it resolves when all promises resolve or rejects if any reject.

questions.question: In a promise chain, what happens when a handler throws an error and how does the chain continue?
questions.goldenAnswer: The thrown error causes the current promise to reject, skipping subsequent .then handlers until a .catch is encountered, which can then handle or recover from the error.

questions.question: Explain the difference between microtasks and macrotasks in the event loop and give an example of when a microtask runs before a macrotask.
questions.goldenAnswer: Microtasks, such as promise callbacks, are processed after the current script but before rendering and before any macrotasks like setTimeout; thus a promise resolution will run before a setTimeout with zero delay.

questions.question: How does async/await change the execution flow compared to using .then, and what role does the event loop play in this change?
questions.goldenAnswer: Async/await is syntactic sugar over promises; awaiting pauses the async function, yielding control to the event loop, which processes pending microtasks before resuming the function.

questions.question: If an async function returns a value, how can callers handle errors that occur inside the function without wrapping the call in try/catch?
questions.goldenAnswer: The async function returns a promise that rejects on error; callers can attach a .catch to the returned promise or use try/catch around the await statement in the caller.

questions.question: When scheduling a promise resolution and a setTimeout with zero delay in the same tick, which callback executes first?
questions.goldenAnswer: The promise resolution callback runs first because promise callbacks are microtasks, which are processed before the macrotask queue where setTimeout callbacks reside.

questions.question: What strategies can you use to effectively cancel a pending promise, and what are the limitations of these strategies?
questions.goldenAnswer: Native promises cannot be cancelled; you can use AbortController with fetch or implement a custom flag to ignore the result, but the underlying operation may still complete.

questions.question: How would you detect and debug a memory leak caused by unresolved promises in a React component?
questions.goldenAnswer: Check for pending promises in componentWillUnmount or useEffect cleanup, ensure promises are resolved or rejected, and use debugging tools or console.trace to identify unhandled promise rejections.

questions.question: In what scenario is Promise.allSettled preferable over Promise.all, and how does it affect error handling?
questions.goldenAnswer: When you need all results regardless of individual failures, Promise.allSettled returns an array of status and value/reason for each promise, preventing a single rejection from aborting the entire batch.

questions.question: When a promise in a chain throws an error, how does the event loop handle the rejection if no catch is attached until a later then?
questions.goldenAnswer: The rejection propagates to the nearest rejection handler; if none is attached until a later then, the rejection is queued as a microtask and will be processed before the next macrotask, potentially causing an unhandled rejection warning if no handler is ever attached.

questions.question: How does async/await transform a function into a promise chain, and how do errors propagate differently compared to explicit promise chaining?
questions.goldenAnswer: async/await is syntactic sugar over promise chains; each await yields a microtask, and any thrown error is automatically wrapped in a rejected promise, so try/catch around await is equivalent to .catch on the promise. Unlike explicit chaining, errors propagate to the nearest async function boundary.

questions.question: What is the difference between setTimeout(fn,0) and Promise.resolve().then(fn) in terms of task queue and microtask queue, and how does that affect UI rendering?
questions.goldenAnswer: setTimeout(fn,0) schedules fn as a macrotask, so it runs after the current stack and all microtasks, whereas Promise.resolve().then(fn) schedules fn as a microtask, running immediately after the current stack but before the next macrotask, allowing faster UI updates.

questions.question: How can you implement a cancellation mechanism for an async function that performs multiple network requests, ensuring that pending promises are properly handled and no memory leaks occur?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use an AbortController to signal cancellation; pass its signal to fetch calls, and reject the async function’s promise when aborted, ensuring no further awaits are processed and no dangling promises remain.

questions.question: How do you create a new array that contains all elements of an existing array plus an additional element, without changing the original array?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the spread operator to build a new array that includes the original elements and the new element.

questions.question: How do you extract the 'title' property from an object into a variable?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use object destructuring: const { title } = obj.

questions.question: How do you merge two objects into a new object without modifying the originals?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the spread operator to create a new object that contains properties from both objects.

questions.question: How do you create a shallow copy of an array?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the slice method or the spread operator to produce a new array that contains the same elements.

questions.question: How do you transform an array of strings into an array of their lengths?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the map method to return the length of each string.

questions.question: How can you create a new array that contains only the 'name' property from an array of user objects?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the map method to iterate over the array and return the name property of each object, producing a new array of names.

questions.question: What is the difference between using the spread operator and concat when combining two arrays?
questions.goldenAnswer: Both create a new array, but spread is more concise and can merge multiple arrays or add elements inline, while concat explicitly takes arrays or values as arguments.

questions.question: How would you merge two objects, ensuring that nested objects are also combined rather than overwritten?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use a deep merge strategy, such as recursively spreading nested objects, or a utility like lodash's merge, to combine properties without overwriting nested structures.

questions.question: Describe how to extract the 'age' and 'city' properties from a user object using destructuring.
questions.goldenAnswer: Declare const {age, city} = user; which assigns the age and city properties to variables of the same name.

questions.question: How can you transform an array of objects into a single object keyed by each object's id?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use reduce to iterate over the array, setting each id as a key and the object as its value in the accumulator.

questions.question: What is a practical way to immutably add a new item to an array stored in React state?
questions.goldenAnswer: Create a new array with the spread operator: setState(prev => [...prev, newItem]); this preserves immutability.

questions.question: Explain how to filter an array of objects to only include those with a property value greater than 10.
questions.goldenAnswer: Apply the filter method with a predicate that checks the property, returning a new array of objects that satisfy the condition.

questions.question: How can you swap the values of two variables without a temporary variable using destructuring?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use array destructuring: [a, b] = [b, a]; this exchanges the values of a and b in a single statement.

questions.question: Explain how you would transform an array of user objects into a lookup map keyed by user ID, ensuring immutability and O(n) time, and discuss trade-offs between using reduce versus forEach.
questions.goldenAnswer: Use Array.reduce to accumulate a new object, returning a new map each iteration to preserve immutability; this gives O(n) time and a single pass, whereas forEach would require mutating a separate accumulator, which is less functional but still O(n).

questions.question: Describe a strategy to merge two deeply nested configuration objects where arrays should be concatenated and objects merged recursively, without mutating the originals.
questions.goldenAnswer: Recursively clone each level, merging objects and concatenating arrays; use spread syntax for shallow copies and a helper that checks types, ensuring immutability and preserving original structures.

questions.question: How would you implement a function that destructures an array of mixed types into named variables while preserving the rest of the array, and what pitfalls should you avoid?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use array destructuring with rest syntax to capture remaining items; avoid assuming fixed positions by checking types before assignment to prevent runtime errors.

questions.question: Explain how to use the spread operator to create a new array that interleaves two existing arrays of equal length, and discuss performance implications compared to a loop.
questions.goldenAnswer: Spread each element into a new array while alternating indices, e.g., using a loop that pushes from both arrays; this avoids creating intermediate arrays and is more efficient than concatenating with spread in a single expression.

questions.question: How do you write a simple arrow function that takes two parameters and returns their sum?
questions.goldenAnswer: Write the parameters in parentheses, then the arrow =>, followed by the expression that adds them. The function will automatically return that value.

questions.question: What keyword do you use to export a function from a JavaScript module?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the export keyword before the function declaration or after it to make the function available to other modules.

questions.question: How can you safely access a deeply nested property without causing an error if an intermediate value is undefined?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the optional chaining operator ?. to chain property accesses; if any part is null or undefined, the whole expression returns undefined.

questions.question: How can you extract multiple properties from an object into separate variables?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use object destructuring by declaring variables inside curly braces and assigning them to the object, which copies the values into the variables.

questions.question: How can you combine two arrays into a new array using ES6 syntax?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the spread operator ... to spread the elements of each array into a new array literal, creating a combined array.

questions.question: Explain how arrow functions differ from traditional function expressions in terms of the this keyword.
questions.goldenAnswer: Arrow functions capture the this value of the enclosing context, so they do not have their own this binding.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the import.meta object in ES modules, and how can it be used?
questions.goldenAnswer: import.meta provides module-specific metadata, such as the module's URL, which can be used for dynamic imports or accessing environment information.

questions.question: Describe how optional chaining can be combined with nullish coalescing to provide default values.
questions.goldenAnswer: You can use optional chaining to safely access a property; if it yields undefined or null, the nullish coalescing operator returns the default value.

questions.question: How does the spread operator work with arrays and objects, and what are the differences?
questions.goldenAnswer: With arrays, the spread operator expands elements into a new array; with objects, it copies enumerable own properties into a new object, but nested objects are still referenced.

questions.question: What are the benefits of using named exports over default exports in ES modules?
questions.goldenAnswer: Named exports allow static analysis, easier refactoring, and prevent accidental re-exports, while default exports can obscure the exported entity.

questions.question: Explain the concept of module resolution in ES6 modules and how it differs from CommonJS.
questions.goldenAnswer: ES6 modules use a strict, static module graph resolved by file extensions and URLs, whereas CommonJS resolves modules at runtime based on the require function.

questions.question: How can you use the optional chaining operator to safely call a method that may not exist?
questions.goldenAnswer: You can append ?. to the method name and then parentheses; if the method is undefined, the expression returns undefined instead of throwing an error.

questions.question: What is the difference between let, const, and var in block scoping and hoisting?
questions.goldenAnswer: let and const are block-scoped and not hoisted to the top of the block, while var is function-scoped and hoisted, leading to potential undefined values before initialization.

questions.question: In a React class component, why might you prefer an arrow function for an event handler over a traditional method, and what caveats should you be aware of when using arrow functions as class methods?
questions.goldenAnswer: Arrow functions capture the lexical this, so the handler automatically has the component instance without manual binding. However, they are created per instance, which can impact performance and memory, and they cannot be used as constructors.

questions.question: When using ES6 modules, how can circular dependencies lead to runtime errors in a frontend application, and what strategies can you employ to mitigate them?
questions.goldenAnswer: Circular imports can result in partially initialized modules, causing undefined values at runtime. To mitigate, refactor shared logic into a separate module, use dynamic imports, or restructure the dependency graph to eliminate cycles.

questions.question: Explain how optional chaining interacts with array access and nullish coalescing, and describe a scenario where this combination might produce an unexpected result.
questions.goldenAnswer: Optional chaining short-circuits when encountering null or undefined, so accessing array[index]?.value returns undefined if the array or element is missing. Combining with nullish coalescing can mask the absence of the array itself, leading to silent failures if the index is out of bounds.

questions.question: How do ES6 static imports enable tree shaking in bundlers, and what pitfalls can arise when using dynamic imports or importing entire libraries?
questions.goldenAnswer: Static imports allow bundlers to analyze and remove unused exports, enabling tree shaking. Dynamic imports or wildcard imports can prevent tree shaking, leading to larger bundles; use named imports and avoid importing whole libraries to mitigate.

questions.question: How do you sort an array of numbers in ascending order in JavaScript?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the array.sort method with a compare function that subtracts the second element from the first to ensure numeric ascending order.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of searching for an element in a sorted array using binary search?
questions.goldenAnswer: Binary search runs in O(log n) time because it repeatedly halves the search space.

questions.question: How can you find the maximum value in an array without using Math.max?
questions.goldenAnswer: Iterate through the array keeping a variable that stores the largest value seen so far and update it whenever a larger element is encountered.

questions.question: What is the difference in time complexity between array.push and array.splice when adding an element at the end?
questions.goldenAnswer: array.push is O(1) because it simply appends, while array.splice at the end is also O(1) but generally splice is O(n) when inserting elsewhere.

questions.question: How would you check if an array contains a specific value?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the array.includes method which returns true if the value is found, otherwise false.

questions.question: You have an array of user objects sorted by last name. How would you efficiently find a user with a specific last name?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use binary search on the sorted array, comparing last names and adjusting low and high pointers until the target is found or the search space is empty.

questions.question: Explain how you would implement a debounce function for a search input to reduce API calls.
questions.goldenAnswer: Create a timer that resets on each keystroke; only trigger the API call after the user stops typing for a specified delay.

questions.question: Given a list of tasks with start and end times, how would you find the maximum number of non-overlapping tasks you can schedule?
questions.goldenAnswer: Sort the tasks by end time and greedily select each task that starts after the last selected task ends, maximizing the count.

questions.question: You need to sort a large dataset of products by price in a web app. What algorithm would you choose and why?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use mergesort for its stable O(n log n) performance and ability to handle large data sets efficiently, or quicksort for in-place sorting with good average performance.

questions.question: Describe how you would detect if a linked list of DOM nodes contains a cycle.
questions.goldenAnswer: Apply Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm with two pointers moving at different speeds; if they ever meet, a cycle exists.

questions.question: You have an array of timestamps and need to find the longest consecutive sequence of days. How would you approach this?
questions.goldenAnswer: Convert timestamps to dates, store them in a set for O(1) lookups, then iterate each date expanding forwards and backwards to count sequence lengths, tracking the maximum.

questions.question: Explain the time complexity of rendering a virtualized list with 10,000 items using a windowing technique.
questions.goldenAnswer: The rendering complexity is O(k), where k is the number of visible items, because only a small window is rendered at any time instead of all 10,000 items.

questions.question: How would you merge two sorted arrays of numbers into one sorted array efficiently?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use a two-pointer merge algorithm that compares the current elements of each array and appends the smaller one to the result, achieving O(n+m) time.

questions.question: You need to implement infinite scrolling for a list of 10 million items in a React app. Describe the algorithmic approach you would use to keep memory usage low and scrolling smooth, including any data structures and complexity considerations.
questions.goldenAnswer: Use virtual scrolling by rendering only a window of items around the viewport, mapping scroll position to index with a linear formula, and loading items on demand; this keeps memory usage proportional to the window size and provides O(1) per scroll event.

questions.question: Explain how you would design a client‑side search feature that supports fuzzy matching and real‑time filtering for a dataset of 500,000 records, focusing on algorithm choice, indexing strategy, and performance trade‑offs.
questions.goldenAnswer: Build a BK‑tree or trie for the dataset, use it to perform fuzzy lookups in O(log n) time, and run the search in a Web Worker to keep the UI responsive; this balances fast queries with acceptable memory overhead.

questions.question: A component must re‑render only when its props change deeply. Propose an algorithm to detect prop changes efficiently, discuss its time complexity, and explain how it compares to shallow comparison in React.
questions.goldenAnswer: Compute a deterministic hash of the props (e.g., via a custom hashing function) and compare hashes; this gives O(n) time per comparison but is faster than recursive deep equality and avoids re‑renders when the hash is unchanged, unlike shallow comparison which only checks references.

questions.question: You are tasked with optimizing the rendering of a large table with dynamic row heights. Describe an algorithm that calculates visible rows and updates the DOM efficiently, including any caching or precomputation techniques and their impact on time and space complexity.
questions.goldenAnswer: Precompute a cumulative height array, binary search to find the first visible row, then render only the rows that fit in the viewport; this gives O(log n) lookup time, O(k) rendering time, and O(n) space for the height cache.

questions.question: How do you write a simple unit test for a function that returns a string using Jest?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use the test or it function to call the function and then use expect to compare the returned string with the expected value.

questions.question: What is the purpose of mocking in unit tests?
questions.goldenAnswer: Mocking replaces real dependencies with controlled substitutes so the unit can be tested in isolation without side effects.

questions.question: How can you mock a module in Jest?
questions.goldenAnswer: Call jest.mock with the module path to replace it with a mock implementation before the test runs.

questions.question: What is Test‑Driven Development and how does it influence writing tests?
questions.goldenAnswer: TDD is writing tests first to define expected behavior, then coding until the tests pass, which guides design and ensures coverage.

questions.question: How do you reset mocks between tests in Jest?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use jest.clearAllMocks or jest.resetAllMocks in a beforeEach hook to ensure each test starts with fresh mock state.

questions.question: How can you mock the global fetch API in Jest to test a component that loads data inside useEffect?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use jest.spyOn on global.fetch and provide a mock implementation that returns a resolved promise with the expected JSON data.

questions.question: How can you test that a debounced function in a component is called only once after rapid user input using Jest timers?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use jest.useFakeTimers, trigger the debounced function multiple times, advance timers by the debounce delay, and assert the function was called only once.

questions.question: What is the simplest way to unit test a Redux reducer with Jest?
questions.goldenAnswer: Call the reducer with an initial state and an action, then compare the returned state to the expected new state.

questions.question: How can you mock a module that exports a class in Jest?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use jest.mock with a factory that returns a mock class constructor and mock methods.

questions.question: How would you test a component that should render a fallback UI when a required prop is undefined?
questions.goldenAnswer: Render the component with the prop set to undefined and verify that the fallback UI or default value is displayed.

questions.question: What is the recommended approach to test async functions with Vitest?
questions.goldenAnswer: Write an async test function, await the async function under test, and assert the resolved value.

questions.question: How do you apply TDD to create a new date formatting utility?
questions.goldenAnswer: Write a failing test that expects a formatted string, implement the function to return the formatted date, then run the test until it passes.

questions.question: How can you mock a custom hook that uses useContext for unit testing a component?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use jest.mock to replace the hook with a mock that returns a predefined context value, then test the component's behavior.

questions.question: How would you design a testable architecture for a component that relies on a third-party analytics SDK, ensuring tests remain deterministic and fast?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use dependency injection to pass a wrapper interface, mock the SDK in tests, and isolate side effects by stubbing the wrapper.

questions.question: In Jest, how would you mock a module that uses dynamic imports and side-effectful initialization, and why is this approach preferable over manual mocking?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use jest.mock with a factory that returns a mock implementation, ensuring the dynamic import is resolved once and side effects are controlled, which keeps test isolation and reduces flakiness.

questions.question: Describe a strategy to test a React hook that internally uses a debounced API call, focusing on timing, cleanup, and avoiding flaky tests.
questions.goldenAnswer: Use fake timers to advance time, assert that the API is called after the debounce delay, and verify cleanup by ensuring no pending timers after unmount.

questions.question: When applying TDD to a complex form with conditional validation rules, how do you structure the tests to avoid duplication while still covering all rule permutations?
questions.goldenAnswer: Create parameterized test cases that iterate over rule combinations, use helper functions to build form state, and assert validation outcomes, keeping tests concise yet exhaustive.

questions.question: How do you retrieve data from a server using the Fetch API?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use fetch with the URL, then chain .then to handle the Promise, parse the response, and use the data.

questions.question: How can you store a simple key-value pair in the browser's local storage?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use localStorage.setItem to store a string value under a key, and retrieve it with localStorage.getItem.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the sessionStorage API and how does it differ from localStorage?
questions.goldenAnswer: sessionStorage keeps data only for the current tab session and is cleared when the tab is closed, while localStorage persists until explicitly cleared.

questions.question: How do you observe when an element enters the viewport using IntersectionObserver?
questions.goldenAnswer: Create an IntersectionObserver with a callback that receives entries, call observe on the target element, and the callback runs when the element's visibility changes.

questions.question: Which browser API would you use to get the user's current geographic location and how?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition, passing a success callback that receives a position object and an optional error callback.

questions.question: How can you cancel an ongoing fetch request when a component unmounts, and why is this important?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use AbortController to signal cancellation. This prevents state updates on unmounted components and avoids memory leaks.

questions.question: When would you choose IndexedDB over localStorage for storing user data?
questions.goldenAnswer: When you need to store large amounts of structured data, perform complex queries, or handle binary blobs. IndexedDB is asynchronous and supports larger storage limits.

questions.question: Explain how IntersectionObserver can be used to implement lazy loading of images and what performance benefits it provides.
questions.goldenAnswer: Observe image placeholders and load the actual image when it enters the viewport. This reduces initial load time and saves bandwidth by only loading visible images.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Service Worker in a web app, and how does it differ from a regular Web Worker?
questions.goldenAnswer: A Service Worker intercepts network requests to enable offline caching and background sync. Unlike a Web Worker, it runs outside the page context and can control multiple pages.

questions.question: How can you leverage the Cache API with fetch to implement a stale-while-revalidate strategy?
questions.goldenAnswer: First return a cached response immediately, then fetch a fresh copy in the background and update the cache. This gives instant data while keeping it up to date.

questions.question: Why might you prefer sessionStorage over cookies for storing a JWT token?
questions.goldenAnswer: SessionStorage is not sent with every request, reducing exposure to CSRF. It also has a larger size limit and is cleared when the tab closes.

questions.question: If new elements are added to the DOM after an IntersectionObserver is created, how do you ensure they are observed?
questions.goldenAnswer: Call observer.observe on each new element or use a MutationObserver to automatically observe added nodes. This keeps the observer tracking dynamic content.

questions.question: How does the Web Animations API improve performance over CSS animations when animating many elements?
questions.goldenAnswer: It runs animations on the compositor thread, reduces layout thrash, and allows fine-grained control over keyframes without forcing reflows.

questions.question: How would you design a fetch retry mechanism that handles transient errors, uses exponential backoff, respects a maximum retry count, and allows the user to cancel the request without leaving dangling promises or UI state?
questions.goldenAnswer: Wrap fetch in a function that tracks retry attempts, applies exponential backoff with jitter, and checks an AbortSignal before each retry; update UI only if the signal is not aborted to avoid stale state.

questions.question: In an SPA that uses IndexedDB for offline caching, how would you design a synchronization strategy that reconciles local changes with a remote server, handles conflict resolution, and ensures consistency across multiple tabs?
questions.goldenAnswer: Use a background sync worker that pushes local changes to the server, listens for server responses, and applies a last-write-wins or operational transform strategy; broadcast changes via BroadcastChannel so all tabs update their IndexedDB and UI atomically.

questions.question: When using IntersectionObserver to lazy-load a large grid of images, what are the trade-offs between using a single observer versus multiple observers, and how would you handle dynamic layout changes such as items being added or removed?
questions.goldenAnswer: A single observer reduces overhead but requires careful rootMargin and threshold tuning; multiple observers can target specific sections but increase memory usage. On layout changes, disconnect and reobserve or use a mutation observer to automatically observe new elements.

questions.question: How would you detect and handle the case where a browser's storage quota is exceeded during a large file upload to IndexedDB, and how would you gracefully degrade the user experience while still allowing the upload to complete?
questions.goldenAnswer: Listen for the quotaExceeded error when writing to IndexedDB, then prompt the user to free space or switch to a temporary in-memory buffer; if the user declines, cancel the upload and show a clear message, ensuring the UI remains responsive.
